## Problem

For $\sigma>0$, define the Gaussian function

$$
f_\sigma(x)
=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}
\exp\left(-\frac{x^2}{2\sigma^2}\right),
\qquad x\in\mathbb R.
$$

Let $T_\sigma$ be the distribution induced by $f_\sigma$:

$$
\langle T_\sigma,\varphi\rangle
=
\int_{\mathbb R}f_\sigma(x)\varphi(x)\,dx,
\qquad
\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R).
$$

Prove that

$$
T_\sigma\longrightarrow\delta_0
$$

in the sense of distributions as $\sigma\to0$.

## Solution

Recall that

$$
T_\sigma\to\delta_0
\quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\mathbb R)
$$

means that for every test function

$$
\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R),
$$

we have

$$
\langle T_\sigma,\varphi\rangle
\longrightarrow
\langle\delta_0,\varphi\rangle
=
\varphi(0).
$$

Let $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$. Then

$$
\langle T_\sigma,\varphi\rangle
=
\int_{\mathbb R}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}
e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}
\varphi(x)\,dx.
$$

Make the change of variables

$$
x=\sigma y.
$$

Then

$$
dx=\sigma\,dy,
$$

and hence

$$
\langle T_\sigma,\varphi\rangle
=
\int_{\mathbb R}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
e^{-y^2/2}
\varphi(\sigma y)\,dy.
$$

For every fixed $y\in\mathbb R$,

$$
\varphi(\sigma y)\to\varphi(0)
$$

as $\sigma\to0$.

Moreover,

$$
|\varphi(\sigma y)|
\leq
\|\varphi\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb R)},
$$

and therefore

$$
\left|
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
e^{-y^2/2}
\varphi(\sigma y)
\right|
\leq
\frac{\|\varphi\|_{L^\infty}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
e^{-y^2/2}.
$$

The function on the right belongs to $L^1(\mathbb R)$. Thus, by the dominated convergence theorem,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lim_{\sigma\to0}
\langle T_\sigma,\varphi\rangle
&=
\int_{\mathbb R}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
e^{-y^2/2}
\varphi(0)\,dy\\
&=
\varphi(0)
\int_{\mathbb R}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
e^{-y^2/2}\,dy.
\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Gaussian is normalized,

$$
\int_{\mathbb R}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
e^{-y^2/2}\,dy
=
1.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\lim_{\sigma\to0}
\langle T_\sigma,\varphi\rangle
=
\varphi(0)
=
\langle\delta_0,\varphi\rangle.
$$

Since this holds for every test function $\varphi$, we conclude that

$$
\boxed{
T_\sigma\longrightarrow\delta_0
\quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\mathbb R).
}
$$

## Remark

The family $\{f_\sigma\}_{\sigma>0}$ is an example of an approximate identity. It satisfies

$$
f_\sigma\geq0,
\qquad
\int_{\mathbb R}f_\sigma(x)\,dx=1,
$$

while its mass becomes increasingly concentrated near the origin as $\sigma\to0$.

Thus the Dirac delta can be understood as the distributional limit of a family of smooth functions, even though $\delta_0$ itself cannot be represented by a locally integrable function.
